prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, reaching unprecedented accuracy and stability in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I opened with circuit QED (B038), but I have to be honest about how that ballot looks from the outside: I was its only supporter, I sit very close to that community, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits was awarded only a year ago. Optical lattice clocks (B049) are the strongest case on the shortlist when judged on the criteria I say I care about. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the Doppler, recoil and Stark-shift problems at once, so that thousands of atoms can be interrogated with every systematic understood in physical detail. The result is fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, independent realizations at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere, and clock comparisons across continents that agree. It has opened genuinely new regimes: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of constant variation, many-body clock physics, and a credible path to redefining the second. It is a clean discovery-plus-instrument story with a natural two-person credit, and four members already place it in their top three. I now prefer it as the configuration to build the prize around.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is history: the 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and precision laser spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single ions, which underlies the best ion clocks. A lattice-clock prize must therefore be justified as a distinct advance (many-atom magic-wavelength interrogation) and not as a continuation of earlier recognition. There is also an attribution issue, because Lemonde, Gill, Lisdat, Ludlow and others made important contributions and Ye's role is as much performance leadership and many-body work as invention. Finally, the value of the work is in measurement, and a prize committee has to be careful that the discovery of a new regime is being rewarded and not merely the best number. If the committee judges that the lattice clock is a refinement of earlier recognized metrology, I would return to circuit QED or to trapped-ion quantum computing.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B049 first, arguing that Katori's proposal and Ye's record performance give a clean two-person prize, with reproduction by many national laboratories, and that the 2005 and 2012 history needs to be handled carefully.
responses.response: I agree on the core and on the clean two-person credit. I would qualify only the framing that this is overdue: the argument that survives the 2005 and 2012 history is that the lattice scheme is a new regime (neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength trap, many-atom interrogation), not that precision metrology has been under-rewarded. I would also resist reading the ion-clock disagreement as settled, since the ion clocks remain competitive at the 1e-18 level. My citation therefore names the lattice invention and its realization explicitly.

responses.point: Lindroth finds B049 the cleanest case for a theorist who values quantitative agreement between theory and experiment: magic-wavelength lattices, a step beyond single-ion clocks, and a stable interpretation.
responses.response: I share that view, and the quantitative control of systematics (blackbody shift, lattice light shifts, density shifts) is for me the decisive virtue. Where I differ slightly is on the competing item you rank second, lattice quantum simulation (B054): the five credited names do not fit three places and the discovery is spread across a long programme, whereas B049 has a compact and defensible credit. I also note your caution that other groups contributed, and I think the committee should say openly that this is a prize for the concept and the first realizations with the accuracy record, not for the whole field.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Daya Bay and RENO theta-13 discovery first as a clean, unambiguous discovery from nature that opened leptonic CP-violation searches, while placing optical lattice clocks only eighth.
responses.response: I take the point that theta-13 is a discovery about nature and not an instrument, and that is a serious argument given that the prize rewards discovery. My difficulty is practical and outside my expertise, so I defer on the physics: with three credited names for experiments of hundreds of members, and Double Chooz and T2K contributing, the attribution seems harder than for lattice clocks, and the 2015 prize on neutrino oscillations makes the distinctness question real. I would like you to say whether you consider Daya Bay and RENO a separate advance from 2015, and whether Double Chooz leadership can be left out. If yes, B024 deserves discussion; I would not hold it in the second tier solely because it is not my field.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics first for exact, universal relations far from equilibrium, and suggests Jarzynski, Evans and Seifert from four credited names.
responses.response: The physics is attractive and I agree that exact relations in small driven systems have been tested in single-molecule, colloidal and, relevant to my own area, electronic and circuit experiments. My reservation is attribution rather than merit: Crooks is a decisive link between theory and experiment, Gallavotti and Cohen are in the background, and the experimentalists such as Bustamante are outside the credited names, so a three-person cut looks contestable. I would like to hear whether you think the theorems are a prize-worthy discovery about nature or a conceptual framework, and who you would drop if the prize had to be strictly three.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether the credit should include other lattice-clock pioneers beyond Katori and Ye, and how to weigh Ye's role (precision and many-body results) against Katori's invention.
Whether a second superconducting-circuit prize (circuit QED) so soon after 2025 is appropriate, and how to allocate four credited names (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin) to three places.
Whether the theta-13 discovery is judged distinct from the 2015 neutrino-oscillation prize, and how its collaboration credit can be fairly cut to three.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work at Chalmers MC2 in superconducting circuits. B038 (circuit QED) and B044 (trapped-ion quantum computing) lie in or adjacent to my programme's field, and WACQT has hosted 2025 laureates and collaborates with groups in quantum technology, so I would recuse myself or at least flag a bias on B038, which I ranked first. I have no specific personal or institutional tie to the B049 candidates (Katori, Ye) apparent from my profile.
